## The question that starts this lesson

> "The journal accepted my paper, but they want a citable version of the code, with a DOI. How do I do that?"

Ten years ago the same question arrived about **datasets**, and libraries built the answer: a persistent identifier, a catalog record, a citation format, a preservation copy. Software mostly hasn't gotten that treatment yet.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**You write research software**, and want to make your own code citable, reusable, and discoverable.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**You support people who do**, as a librarian, OSPO member, or research-support specialist.
:::

::::

**Supporting others** slides translate each step into consultation work.

::: {.notes}
This is a real question faculty ask. Lead with it — researchers don't adopt these
practices because they're virtuous, they adopt them because journals are starting to
require citable code deposits, funders ask, and a DOI turns invisible labor into a
countable, citable output for their CV. This is credit they're currently leaving on
the table. The hands-on steps that follow are the same regardless of which audience
you're in.
:::

## How common is the software citation gap?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### 59.5%

of 3.2 million PubMed Central articles mention at least one piece of software
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### 38%

of 2020 articles give enough detail to **uniquely identify** the software they used
:::

::::

::: {.small}
Both figures: Schindler et al. (2022), PeerJ Computer Science, doi:10.7717/peerj-cs.835
:::

## A GitHub URL isn't a citation

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### ❌ Wrong

> "We used the analysis script from github.com/UC-OSPO-Network/software-demo"

- Links rot
- No version: which code produced the result?
- No author, so no credit
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### ✅ Right

> Dennis, T., Phan, L., Otsuji, R., & Padilla, K. (2026). *Biodiversity Analysis Toolkit* (v0.1.0). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.123456

- The DOI outlives the repo
- The version is explicit
- Authors get credit and citation counts
:::

::::

You'll create both pieces today: a `CITATION.cff` file and a DOI.

::: {.notes}
A URL is a shelf location, not a catalog record. Citing code this way is like citing
a book as "third shelf, Powell Library reading room." Move the book, close the room,
the reference is dead. Gitorious shut down in 2015, Google Code in 2016, thousands
of projects unreachable overnight.

The DOI here is illustrative, in real Zenodo format (10.5281). Learners mint on
Zenodo Sandbox today, so theirs will start 10.5072 and won't resolve on doi.org.
That's expected for practice.

If there's time, the durability story: before Heartbleed (2014), OpenSSL secured
about a sixth of the web's encrypted traffic on ~$2,000/year in donations with one
paid maintainer. Depositing in an archive moves software off one person's account.
:::

## Where your fork is headed

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Before (`main`)

- ❌ No LICENSE
- ❌ No citation information
- ❌ No release or DOI
- ❌ Minimal README
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
### After (`05-add-metadata`)

- ✅ LICENSE (BSD-3-Clause) · *Reusable*
- ✅ CITATION.cff · *Findable*
- ✅ Release + DOI on Zenodo · *Findable, Accessible*
- ✅ Full README, CONTRIBUTING, Code of Conduct · *Reusable*
:::

::::

**Today:** 2 License → 3 CITATION.cff → 4 Release + DOI → 5 Metadata → wrap-up

::: {.small}
The labels come from FAIR4RS: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable. Check your work any time against the matching reference branch (`02-add-license` … `05-add-metadata`) in the upstream repo.
:::

::: {.notes}
Keep FAIR light: a preview, not a lecture. Learners understand the letters better
after they build each piece. Name the arc and move on.

Optional real-world example if someone asks what "good" looks like at scale:
Spack (github.com/spack/spack) has a clear README, Apache-2.0 or MIT license,
CITATION.cff, docs, and a code of conduct and contributing guide.
:::

## Fork the demo repository

Every hands-on step happens in **your own fork**, not the shared demo repo.

1. Open `github.com/UC-OSPO-Network/software-demo`
2. Click **Fork** → **Create fork** (defaults are fine — `main` branch only)
3. Confirm the top-left reads **`YOUR-USERNAME/software-demo`**, not `UC-OSPO-Network/software-demo`

::: {.small}
Reference branches are there to check your work, never to build on. Full setup details: ucospo.net/research-software-citable-discoverable/learners/setup
:::

::: {.notes}
Before learners begin, ask everyone to confirm the top-left path says
THEIR-USERNAME/software-demo. Have helpers check chat/room for anyone still on the
upstream repository. Do not continue until most learners are in their own fork.
:::

## The starting point

::: {style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
software-demo/
├── README.md
├── requirements.txt
└── src/
    └── analysis.py
```
:::

Deliberately bare. By the end it will have a license, citation metadata, a DOI, and a real README.

::: {.notes}
Ask learners to confirm they see exactly these three items in their fork. This is
the best early moment to catch anyone on the wrong repository, wrong branch, or not
signed in.
:::

## Supporting others: a four-question triage {background-color="#f0f4fa"}

**Public is not the same as shared.** When a researcher brings you their repo, do a fast triage, not a code review.

1. **Rights** — is there a license? Can this legally be reused at all?
2. **Credit** — can a stranger tell who made it and how to cite it?
3. **Runnable** — is there any record of what it takes to run?
4. **Findable** — would anyone outside the lab ever discover it?

The goal is the **single highest-value next step**, not fixing everything.

**Try it now (2 min):** answer all four for your fork of `software-demo`.

::: {.notes}
Think of a bare repo as an unprocessed accession: in the building, not in the
collection. Technically held, practically invisible.

Most repos need one or two changes to go from unusable to useful, and your value is
helping the researcher see which one. That ordering is the whole skill — and it's
one this audience already has from appraising every other kind of material. This
four-question framing is also the take-home tool: the five-minute consultation
format the whole lesson builds toward. Give them the full two minutes before moving on.
:::

## Key points

- A GitHub URL is not a citation. A DOI is permanent and version-specific.
- Software that isn't deposited anywhere depends on one person and one platform
- FAIR4RS (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) is the framework
- Public is not the same as shared: license, citation, and description do the work

::: {.notes}
Wrap this block and hand off to the next presenter for the License episode. Remind
the room the reference branches are there the whole time if anyone falls behind.
